name: Physics
description: A draft progression through measurement, mechanics, waves, and introductory electricity.

resources.title: Measurement and Units: visual preview
resources.body: Draft storyboard activity: sketch and narrate one core measurement and units idea; this label does not refer to a published video.

resources.title: Measurement and Units: guided practice
resources.body: Original self-guided activity: work through a short measurement and units example and check each reasoning step; this is a learning prompt, not an external resource.

questions.text: What is the SI base unit of length?
questions.explanation: The meter is the SI base unit for length.

questions.text: How many meters are in 3 kilometers?
questions.explanation: A kilometer is 1,000 meters, so 3 km = 3,000 m.

questions.text: Which quantity is a scalar?
questions.explanation: Mass has magnitude only; the other listed quantities have direction.

questions.text: A measurement is 12.0 cm. What does the trailing zero communicate?
options: The measurement is recorded to the tenths place
questions.explanation: A trailing zero after the decimal indicates reported precision to 0.1 cm.

questions.text: Which SI base-unit combination is equivalent to one joule?
questions.explanation: A joule is a newton-meter: (kg·m/s²)·m = kg·m²/s².

questions.text: What is 250 milligrams in grams?
questions.explanation: There are 1,000 mg per gram, so 250 mg = 0.25 g.

questions.text: Which dimension describes speed?
questions.explanation: Speed is distance traveled divided by elapsed time.

questions.text: A quantity is 5 m/s. What is its value in km/h?
questions.explanation: Multiply by 3.6 to convert m/s to km/h: 5 × 3.6 = 18.

resources.title: Motion: visual preview
resources.body: Draft storyboard activity: sketch and narrate one core motion idea; this label does not refer to a published video.

resources.title: Motion: guided practice
resources.body: Original self-guided activity: work through a short motion example and check each reasoning step; this is a learning prompt, not an external resource.

questions.text: A runner travels 100 m in 20 s. What is the average speed?
questions.explanation: Average speed is distance divided by time: 100/20 = 5 m/s.

questions.text: An object’s position changes from 3 m to 11 m east. What is its displacement?
questions.explanation: Displacement is final position minus initial position: 11 - 3 = 8 m east.

questions.text: A car speeds up from 4 m/s to 10 m/s in 3 s. What is its average acceleration?
questions.explanation: Acceleration is change in velocity over time: (10-4)/3 = 2 m/s².

questions.text: An object is dropped from rest, ignoring air resistance. What is its velocity after 2 s near Earth (g≈9.8 m/s²)?
questions.explanation: The change in velocity is gt ≈ 9.8×2 = 19.6 m/s downward.

questions.text: An object moves at constant velocity. What is its acceleration?
questions.explanation: Constant velocity means no change in velocity, so acceleration is zero.

questions.text: On a position-time graph, what does the slope represent?
questions.explanation: Slope is change in position divided by time, which is velocity.

questions.text: A cyclist covers 30 km in 2 h. What is the average speed?
questions.explanation: Average speed equals total distance divided by total time: 30/2 = 15 km/h.

questions.text: A ball is thrown straight up. At its highest point, ignoring air resistance, what is true?
options: Its velocity is zero momentarily and acceleration is downward
Both velocity and acceleration are zero
Its velocity is upward and acceleration is zero
questions.explanation: At the peak its vertical velocity is momentarily zero, but gravity still accelerates it downward.

resources.title: Forces and Newton’s Laws: visual preview
resources.body: Draft storyboard activity: sketch and narrate one core forces and newton’s laws idea; this label does not refer to a published video.

resources.title: Forces and Newton’s Laws: guided practice
resources.body: Original self-guided activity: work through a short forces and newton’s laws example and check each reasoning step; this is a learning prompt, not an external resource.

questions.text: What is the SI unit of force?
questions.explanation: Force is measured in newtons (N).

questions.text: A net force of 12 N acts on a 3 kg object. What is its acceleration?
questions.explanation: Newton’s second law gives a = F/m = 12/3 = 4 m/s².

questions.text: A book rests on a table. Which force balances its weight vertically?
questions.explanation: The table exerts an upward normal force equal to the book’s weight at rest.

questions.text: If the net force on an object is zero, what does Newton’s first law say?
questions.explanation: Zero net force means no acceleration, so velocity stays constant.

questions.text: A 2 kg object accelerates at 3 m/s². What is the net force?
questions.explanation: Newton’s second law gives F = ma = 2×3 = 6 N.

questions.text: What is the approximate weight of a 5 kg mass near Earth (g≈9.8 m/s²)?
questions.explanation: Weight is mg: 5×9.8 = 49 N.

questions.text: When you push a wall, what is the Newton’s-third-law partner to your push?
options: The wall pushes you with an equal and opposite force
questions.explanation: Interaction forces occur in equal and opposite pairs on different objects.

questions.text: A 10 kg cart has 30 N forward and 10 N backward forces. What is its acceleration?
questions.explanation: The net force is 20 N forward, so a = 20/10 = 2 m/s² forward.

resources.title: Work, Energy, and Power: visual preview
resources.body: Draft storyboard activity: sketch and narrate one core work, energy, and power idea; this label does not refer to a published video.

resources.title: Work, Energy, and Power: guided practice
resources.body: Original self-guided activity: work through a short work, energy, and power example and check each reasoning step; this is a learning prompt, not an external resource.

questions.text: What is the SI unit of energy?
questions.explanation: Energy is measured in joules.

questions.text: A 10 N force moves an object 3 m in the force direction. How much work is done?
questions.explanation: Work is force times displacement along the force: 10×3 = 30 J.

questions.text: What is the kinetic energy of a 2 kg object moving at 3 m/s?
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy is ½mv² = ½×2×9 = 9 J.

questions.text: A 2 kg object is lifted 5 m. Approximately how much gravitational potential energy does it gain (g≈10 m/s²)?
questions.explanation: The gain is mgh = 2×10×5 = 100 J.

questions.text: A machine transfers 600 J of energy in 20 s. What is its average power?
questions.explanation: Power is energy transferred per time: 600/20 = 30 W.

questions.text: If an object’s speed doubles, by what factor does its kinetic energy change?
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy is proportional to speed squared, so doubling speed gives four times the energy.

questions.text: In an ideal isolated system, what happens to total energy?
questions.explanation: Energy can change forms, but total energy remains constant in an isolated system.

questions.text: A 100 W lamp runs for 60 s. How much energy does it use?
questions.explanation: Energy = power × time = 100×60 = 6,000 J.

resources.body: Draft storyboard activity: sketch and narrate one core waves and sound idea; this label does not refer to a published video.

resources.title: Waves and Sound: guided practice
resources.body: Original self-guided activity: work through a short waves and sound example and check each reasoning step; this is a learning prompt, not an external resource.

questions.text: What is the SI unit of frequency?
questions.explanation: Frequency is measured in hertz, equivalent to cycles per second.

questions.text: A wave has frequency 5 Hz and wavelength 2 m. What is its speed?
questions.explanation: Wave speed is frequency times wavelength: 5×2 = 10 m/s.

questions.text: In a transverse wave, particle motion is what relative to the direction of travel?
questions.explanation: Transverse oscillations are perpendicular to the wave’s propagation direction.

questions.text: A sound wave travels through air. What kind of wave is it?
questions.explanation: Sound in air is a mechanical longitudinal wave of compressions and rarefactions.

questions.text: If a wave’s frequency doubles while its speed in the same medium stays fixed, what happens to its wavelength?
questions.explanation: Since v=fλ and v is fixed, doubling f halves λ.

questions.text: What does a wave’s amplitude generally describe?
questions.explanation: Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the equilibrium position.

questions.text: What is the period of a wave with frequency 4 Hz?
questions.explanation: Period T is the reciprocal of frequency: T=1/4 s.

questions.text: Why can sound not travel through a vacuum?
options: It requires a material medium to transmit vibrations
questions.explanation: Sound is mechanical and needs particles to pass on pressure disturbances.

resources.body: Draft storyboard activity: sketch and narrate one core electricity and magnetism idea; this label does not refer to a published video.

resources.title: Electricity and Magnetism: guided practice
resources.body: Original self-guided activity: work through a short electricity and magnetism example and check each reasoning step; this is a learning prompt, not an external resource.

questions.text: What is the SI unit of electric current?
questions.explanation: Electric current is measured in amperes.

questions.text: A 6 V battery is connected across a 3 Ω resistor. What current flows?
questions.explanation: Ohm’s law gives I=V/R=6/3=2 A.

questions.text: Two positive electric charges placed near each other exert what kind of force?
questions.explanation: Like electric charges repel.

questions.text: In a simple series circuit, what happens to current through each component?
options: It is the same through each component
It is zero after the first component
It depends only on wire color
questions.explanation: A series circuit has one path, so the same current passes through each component.

questions.text: Two resistors of 6 Ω and 3 Ω are connected in parallel. What is their equivalent resistance?
questions.explanation: For parallel resistors, 1/R=1/6+1/3=1/2, so R=2 Ω.

questions.text: What is the SI unit of electric charge?
questions.explanation: Electric charge is measured in coulombs.

questions.text: What happens to the magnetic field around a straight wire if its current increases?
questions.explanation: The magnetic field magnitude around the wire is proportional to current.

questions.text: A device has 12 V across it and carries 0.5 A. What is its electrical power?
questions.explanation: Electrical power is P=VI=12×0.5=6 W.
